UK Jobs Market: Hiring is slowing, but British industry has a much bigger problem coming.

The latest KPMG/REC Report on Jobs landed this morning. Permanent placements are falling, temporary hiring has contracted and candidate availability continues to increase. Yet IT, Computing and Engineering are leading the sectors for growth in permanent staff demand.

As founder of EMBS Group, I'm seeing a slightly different picture emerging across the specialist markets we serve.

We're seeing more vacancies being signed off, more genuine hiring commitments and an increase in contract opportunities, particularly outside IR35. AI is also creating significant demand for new skills, from agentic engineering to the integration of AI into products, manufacturing and business operations.

But my biggest concern is what's happening in UK manufacturing, particularly defence and aerospace.

This weekend's Rolls-Royce announcement really brought the scale of the challenge into focus.

The INFINITY technology park development in Derby, expected to support 17,500 skilled jobs, is fantastic news for the region. Add the wider investment in defence, nuclear and aerospace, and we're looking at enormous opportunities for British industry.
But where are all these skilled people coming from?

We're already seeing acute shortages of CNC machinists, programmers, mechanical fitters, technicians and experienced production engineers.

And here's the problem. Too much recruitment activity simply moves experienced people between employers. One manufacturer fills a vacancy, another inherits the shortage. Salaries rise, recruitment costs increase, but we haven't created a single additional skilled worker.

We're redistributing a skills shortage rather than solving it.
We need government, employers, education providers and the recruitment industry working together. More apprenticeships, adult retraining, technical education and serious investment in reskilling existing workforces.

And we need to recognise something else.

Yes, AI is changing jobs, workflows and productivity at an extraordinary pace. But Elon's robots haven't arrived on our factory floors just yet!

We still need humans. Skilled humans. And we need an awful lot more of them, FAST.
The irony is that while we're debating how many jobs AI might replace, some of our most strategically important industries can't find enough people to deliver the work already coming through the door.

AI will improve manufacturing productivity, but it won't eliminate the need for experienced engineers, machinists and skilled tradespeople any time soon.

My conclusion?
The UK jobs market may be fragile, but the opportunities in AI, defence, aerospace and advanced manufacturing are substantial. The challenge isn't simply winning contracts or attracting investment. It's developing the workforce capable of delivering them.
Recruitment moves talent. Training creates it.

And British industry desperately needs to start creating more.

On paper, it should be getting easier to hire.

But more CVs isn’t the same as more of the right people.

The specialist end of tech is still busy. Demand for contract tech staff hit its highest level since January 2023 in September, and a lot of it is AI-related.

And “AI experience” on a CV covers a lot of ground. A short course and two years running models in production can look identical on paper.

If your applications have picked up, a few things worth tightening:

➡️ Be clear in the advert about what the role has to deliver
➡️ Screen for what someone has built and shipped, not the keywords
➡️ Ask what went wrong and what they changed - that usually separates the two
➡️ Don’t assume a bigger pile means a lower salary. The specialists still have options

A busier inbox can make hiring slower, not faster.

You cannot layer autonomous AI agents onto a legacy foundation.

The contact center stack as we know it is running on borrowed time.

For decades, the standard playbook for enterprise CX was simple: pick a legacy CCaaS vendor, lock into a 3-to-5-year contract, and spend millions hiring specialized developers to write custom pro-code integrations for basic routing.

It created massive vendor lock-in and technical debt. 

But worse, it created an architectural bottleneck.

Now, every enterprise wants "Agentic AI." 

But here is the hard truth: You cannot layer autonomous AI agents onto a legacy foundation that relies on rigid, custom-coded routing rules.

The industry is splitting into two clear camps:
- The Rip-and-Replace Trap
Legacy vendors pushing full platform overhauls just to access basic GenAI add-ons.

- The Intelligence Layer
Architecture that sits directly on top of existing infrastructure, bringing native AI agents, real-time quality management, and rich business context without tearing down core routing on day one.

The future isn't about writing 10,000 lines of custom code to bridge your CRM and your contact center. 

It's about unified platforms where low-code orchestration, native CRM context, and AI agents run on the exact same foundation.

Architectural agility beats custom code every single time.

Fewer frontend jobs?
Fewer jobs for frontend that only does layout.

Looking at the market this year, I see two things at once.

Roles like "build screens from Figma" are shrinking. AI drafts a decent component from a design in minutes, and companies noticed.

At the same time, the frontend roles that stay open ask for much more:
• architecture of a large client app, not just components
• API contracts, auth flows, payments, realtime data
• performance on real devices, not just Lighthouse on a MacBook
• CI/CD, feature flags, releases, monitoring in production
• often mobile too: React Native, sometimes native Swift or Kotlin

That's not "frontend is dying". That's frontend growing into what it always was in good teams: the engineer responsible for everything the user touches.

In my projects, the hardest problems were never "how do I center this". They were: why does checkout fail on one Android version only, how do we roll out a new auth flow without logging everyone out, how do we keep a trading UI responsive under a firehose of price updates.

Layout skills are now the floor, not the ceiling. The ceiling is owning the full cycle.

The hardest renewal to rescue is when an enterprise client experiences a sudden 30% workforce layoff 60 days before contract signature. 

With two months left on a $290K enterprise agreement covering 400 core seats, the client executed a massive corporate restructuring that eliminated 120 employees, prompting their Chief People Officer and Procurement lead to demand an immediate $90K contract reduction to reflect their shrunken team. Caving to the cut meant absorbing a massive hit to net revenue retention, while enforcing the strict contract minimums on an executive team in crisis would guarantee they would churn completely at the next cycle. Instead of debating contract clauses or passively taking the 30% contraction, I audited their post-layoff platform telemetry and discovered that the remaining 280 employees were drowning in manual operational workload, struggling to maintain the same customer output with nearly a third of their teammates gone. I met with their COO and proposed an executive pivot: rather than leaving their remaining staff stranded or taking a flat seat reduction, we converted their legacy seat-based contract into an automated enterprise workflow tier that bundled our advanced AI orchestration and bulk data processing modules for the remaining 280 users, alongside a multi-year ramped agreement locking in spend at $275K ARR (a minor 5% adjustment instead of a 30% collapse) with guaranteed price protection when they resumed hiring. The COO recognized that the automation features were vital to preventing employee burnout among the retained team and secured board approval within ten days, protecting 95% of our revenue baseline during an existential client crisis.

When a customer’s sudden layoffs threaten your seat-based contract, how do you protect your ARR without appearing indifferent to their situation? 👇

After working with more than 100 students and graduates, I keep seeing the same mistake made time and time again. 

People apply before they are ready to apply.

Sending 50 - 100 applications to a massive variety of roles, company sizes, and with little to not tailoring. They use one cover letter for every employer. They apply for roles without understanding what the company does, who it serves or why the role exists.

Companies get these often AI-generated generic applications, and rightfully so reject them on mass to get to the applications that speak directly to them as an employer. 

Candidates do not get feedback as it's logistically impossible for overworked recruitment teams to give this, then candidates blame everything other than the quality of the applications that they make. 

This isn't to say that it's not a bad job market, an inefficient hiring system, or at times lazy company practices which place my generation at a difficult point. But you must focus on what you can control which is: 

- The quality of your application materials, so your CV, CL, portfolio, and Loom video pitches. 

- The extent to which you tailor your job applications to the job description and company. 

- The strategy you use to apply, so the a combo of entry-level, graduate schemes, contract-to-hire, and other role types.

Heidi : what happens when the money arrives before the market does

In September, Heidi looked like Australia’s next great health tech success. The Melbourne company, which makes AI clinical notes software, raised US$100m in a Series C led by Blackbird at a valuation of A$1.26bn. It added a US$240m growth facility from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, which is money set aside to pay for customer acquisition. It was named Scaleup of the Year. It supports around three million patient interactions a week.

Six weeks later, Heidi told staff it was cutting about 18% of its global workforce, more than 100 people from a team of over 600. Two of its three co-founders, CTO Yu Liu and CFO Waleed Mussa, announced they were stepping back. The news landed the same week Canva cut 22% of its staff.

So what changed in six weeks? Very little, and that’s the point. The forces behind these cuts were there all along.

1. Hospitals buy slowly, whatever your hiring plan says
CEO Dr Tom Kelly was candid. Heidi had been “too optimistic” about how quickly large health systems would buy, and had hired too many enterprise staff for hospital deals that moved slowly. Anyone who has sold into the NHS or a council will recognise this. Wales has just abandoned a £10m procurement for ambient voice technology, saying too few suppliers met the requirements. North West London is tendering for a contract that won’t start until April 2027. Health and care budgets move on a timetable of their own, and venture capital rarely shares it.

2. Investors now want predictable revenue, not just growth
Kelly said investors wanted a “more forecastable” business. A debt facility tied to customer acquisition comes with an expectation that every pound spent brings back a customer, on a schedule. Two years ago, a company growing as fast as Heidi could hire ahead of demand and expect the next round to cover it. That tolerance has gone.

3. AI on its own is not a moat
Most AI scribes rent their models from the same handful of providers. In February, Epic, which runs the records systems in many large US hospitals, launched its own scribe. When the platform you sit on top of builds your product into its own, your advantage has to come from somewhere else: distribution, data, trust or integration.

4. Access to the record matters more than the AI
Heidi doesn’t have a deep integration deal with the major GP and hospital record vendors, and one vendor described its partnership with Heidi as bringing negligible revenue. Its public dispute with Best Practice Software, a leading Australian GP software vendor, showed how much depends on access to the record. A note-taking tool that can’t write cleanly into the system clinicians use every day is always one step from the workflow.

5. Talent costs money in both directions
Heidi’s funding let it hire aggressively, and local incumbents say this pushed up salaries across the sector. The cuts reportedly hit R&D, support and sales in Melbourne, with some roles moving offshore. Those people will now be hired by steadier players, which is good news for the incumbents who were losing staff to Heidi a year ago.

What this means for care technology in the UK
None of this means Heidi is in trouble. It is still growing, and the restructure moves customer support closer to product and puts R&D under one roadmap, which is sensible. What it shows is the gap between how fast technology can scale and how fast health and care organisations can adopt it.

For care tech suppliers here, the lessons are practical:
- Plan for the buying cycle you have, not the one in the pitch deck
- Integrate with the systems providers already use, especially digital social care records, before chasing new markets
- Build revenue you can forecast, because that is what investors are now paying for
- Treat AI as a feature people buy for the outcome, not the reason they buy

The companies that last will be the ones that understand how care is actually commissioned, bought and delivered. The money only buys time to work that out.

Day 3/20 | Same AI, Different Risk

Yesterday: two dials show how hard a deal is. Today: the AI's output decides what the deal must cover. 

The answer: the type of output changes which risks the contract has to cover [Ray Sun, Oct 2026].

Content outputs (text, images, code): the main worries are IP infringement and misuse by users. Decision outputs (hiring, credit, insurance): the main worries are bias and the effect on people. 

The content side has some answers. In 2023 Microsoft, Google and OpenAI each offered IP indemnities for outputs of their own AI products, with conditions [Addleshaw Goddard, Nov 2023].

The decision side looks thinner. If a tool produces biased or discriminatory outputs, vendors typically disclaim responsibility [Bennett Jones, Nov 2025]. The EU AI Act treats credit scoring (except fraud detection) and life and health insurance pricing as high-risk, with duties due from 2 December 2027.

I feel the gap follows control, as in Day 2. A vendor that built its model controls what it was trained on, so it can stand behind IP claims. It controls less over who a bank scores with it, or what the bank does with the result. That fits what I found: protection for IP claims, disclaimers for biased decisions.

I feel this is where the two output types really split. You can read a drafted letter and see what it says. You can't read a loan refusal and see why it came out that way. A bank cannot check what it cannot see.

The finance parallel: US bank guidance on model risk covers models a bank buys, not only models it builds, and was revised in April 2026. But the revised version says generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance" [OCC Bulletin 2026-13, Apr 2026]. And many AI agreements do not commit vendors to transparency, so vendors are not required to provide audit reports or documentation of model logic [Bennett Jones, Nov 2025].

For models in scope, the bank has guidance telling it to check vendor products. For generative and agentic AI, that guidance steps aside, and the contract often does not require the evidence either. I feel that leaves the bank with less to lean on unless it writes the right to documentation into the contract. A hypothetical: an agentic AI tool screens loan applications and turns one down, and the bank is asked to explain why. If the contract never gave the bank documentation, it has nothing to explain with.

For vendors my suggestion is that, if you already split your terms by output type and offer model documentation for decisions about people, say so up front. Customers read your contract to judge your AI governance.

Your most valuable sales data probably lives in tools you rent.

Contacts sit in the CRM. Company facts sit with the data provider. Buying signals sit in another tool. Email history sits in the outreach tool. Each one holds a piece, in its own format, under its own contract.

Switch one tool and a piece of your history leaves with it.

So I keep the core in a plain database the company owns. Accounts, people, signals, and what happened with each. Nothing fancy: a table per thing, with a clear key.

The tools plug in around it. They read what they need and write back what they learn. The CRM becomes the window sales works in. The ad platforms get their audiences from it. Outreach gets its lists from it.

Three things change when you work this way.
- Switching tools becomes a small job. The history stays put.
- You can ask questions across everything, like "which accounts we lost last year are hiring again?"
- AI agents get one place to read from, with clear rules about what they can touch.

It sounds like more work. In practice it's less, because every new tool plugs into the same place.

Tools come and go. The data in the middle should stay yours.

Employers increasingly use AI tools to screen CVs, rank candidates and assess applicants, and these tools process personal data covered by Kenya’s 

Data Protection Act, 2019. Section 35 gives a person the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, where the decision has legal effects or significantly affects them, subject to exceptions for contract necessity, authorising law with safeguards, and consent. 

Where such a decision is made, the person must be notified in writing and can ask for it to be reconsidered or for a new decision not based solely on automated processing. Regulation 22 of the Data Protection (General) Regulations, 2021 also requires meaningful information about the logic involved, an explanation of the likely consequences, steps to address bias, and human intervention. 

Employers and HR teams should review whether their hiring tools decide without human involvement and what applicants are told, and applicants should know they can ask for a decision to be reconsidered.

Your LLM can read 1 million tokens. So why does it still get your own documents wrong?

I have spent the last few months building RAG systems and multi-agent workflows in Django and Python, and the pattern keeps repeating: the model is rarely the problem. The document is.

Real business documents are messy. A policy PDF that references a spreadsheet. A contract with the key clause buried in an appendix. A CV where the most important experience is implied, never stated. Feed all of that into a long context window and the model will still miss things — not because it cannot read, but because it cannot tell what matters.

Three things I have learned the hard way:

1. Retrieval beats length. A well-chunked, well-ranked retrieval layer over 50 pages outperforms a raw 500-page dump every time. Relevance is a design decision, not a token count.

2. Structure is a feature. Headings, tables, dates, versions — when you preserve them instead of flattening a document into plain text, the model reasons far better.

3. The last mile is verification. Every generated answer that touches a real decision needs a trace back to the source passage. If a hiring manager or a customer cannot check where an answer came from, they should not trust it.

Long context is a wonderful capability. But treating it as a substitute for good retrieval, clean structure and verification is how teams ship impressive demos and unreliable products.

For the leaders here — CEOs, Directors, HR heads — when you evaluate an AI tool for your team, what do you look for first: the size of the context window, or proof that its answers can be traced back to your own documents?
